subtype: Approach: thinking of what the test is for [Thinking]
passage: Vishal's friend Zainab tapped his shoulder before the fractions test and mouthed, "Answers?" Vishal's pencil hovered. It would be easy. Two minutes, and she would get her marks. But then what? If she copies, the teacher thinks she knows fractions. Next chapter is ratios, and fractions sit inside ratios. She will be lost, and I will have helped her get lost. Marks would come today; learning would not. He turned his paper a little, shook his head and whispered, "I will help you learn it after school. Copying will not help you." Zainab sighed but nodded. Vishal felt his hands go steady.

qa.q: Which chapter did Vishal think would come after fractions?
qa.a: Vishal thought the next chapter would be ratios.

qa.q: How was Vishal feeling while his pencil hovered, and what made him decide?
qa.a: Whether giving Zainab the answers truly helps her, and he realised it would give marks without learning, so he felt torn but chose to refuse. 😅

qa.q: What other approach could Vishal use to help Zainab?
qa.a: Offer to study together after school, because then she learns the method she needs for the next chapter.

qa.q: How might Zainab see Vishal's refusal?
qa.a: Disappointed at first, since she sighed, but she nodded, so she may come to see that he wants her to understand.

grounding: A boy reasons that copying gives marks but no learning, so helping a friend cheat does not truly help.

passage:
"Gurpreet, pass me your answers in the test tomorrow. Just the algebra part."
"No, Pradeep."
"Why? We're friends."
"Because we're friends. Think. If you copy tomorrow, you get marks. Then what?"
"Then I pass."
"And next month is equations. Equations are built on algebra. You'll sit there and nothing will make sense, and I won't be next to you in the half-yearly."
"So you won't help me."
"I didn't say that. Copying isn't helping; it just hides the problem for one day. Come over tonight. We'll do ten sums."
"Ten?"
"Fine. Eight. With chai."
Pradeep laughed in spite of himself. "Seven o'clock?"
"Seven."

qa.q: Which part did Pradeep want to copy?
What was Gurpreet worried about when he asked 'Then what?'
qa.a: He was worried that copying would leave Pradeep lost when equations came next month.

qa.q: What else could Gurpreet offer if one evening isn't enough?
qa.a: A few short sessions before the half-yearly, so Pradeep builds the algebra properly.
From pushing for answers to laughing in spite of himself and agreeing to study.

grounding: A boy reasons aloud that copying gives marks but no learning, so helping a friend cheat would not really help him.

passage: Last year, during the science unit test, my friend Baljeet whispered, "Sachin, tilt your paper. Just a little." I remember my hand actually starting to move. Then I thought: the test is on electricity. Next month we build circuits in the lab, in pairs. If Baljeet copies my answers now, he'll get a good mark and still not know what a closed circuit is. Then in the lab he'll be lost, and I'll be doing it all. So I didn't tilt my paper. After the test he was angry. I told him, "Copying gives you marks, not the knowing. Sit with me on Saturday." He came, grumbling. In the lab next month, he was the one who got our bulb to light.

qa.q: How did Sachin feel when Baljeet whispered?
qa.a: Tempted at first, with a hand starting to move, then uneasy as the thinking began.

qa.q: What else could Sachin have done after the test?
qa.a: Explained the reason to Baljeet calmly, as happened, and offered more than one study session.

qa.q: How does Baljeet seem to feel over time?
qa.a: Angry right after the test, grumbling on Saturday, and then proud when he got the bulb to light.

grounding: Looking back, a child reasons that copying gives marks but no learning, so letting a friend copy would not truly help him.
